title: Health rebate cut impact ‘set to soar’
full_text:
Health Minister Mark Butler’s own department has forecast the number of older Australians dumping health insurance under Labor’s rebate cut will be nearly double the figure the government regularly quotes by the end of the decade.
Analysis from the Department of Health, Disability and Ageing shows the widely claimed government figure that only 44,000 Australians would dump private health insurance under the policy would blow out to 78,000 just a year later.
The documents, obtained under a freedom of information request, show the 44,000 figure consistently quoted by Labor was forecast for the year 2028-29, with the department admitting it expected this to rise significantly in 2029-30.
With the Coalition staunchly against the proposal and the Greens unlikely support it through parliament without amendments, the department documents show the 44,000 estimate “represents the initial effect of the policy at any point in time”.
After 2028-29 when the policy has been up and running for two years, the department expects “individuals aged 65-plus continue to have a higher likelihood of downgrading or exiting cover under the new rebate settings”.
“These behavioural responses compound over time, progressively widening the gap relative to the baseline. As a result, the difference (between insurance coverage due to the policy change) increases to around 78,000 by 2029-30,” the documents say. “As a result, overall participation continues to grow … but at a slower rate than under the baseline.” The department explains it uses the 44,000 figure publicly because the “minor impacts” from the policy are expected to be the most pronounced in its first two years.
The documents say modelling beyond 2028-29 decreases over time “as assumptions about behaviour, economic conditions and policy settings become less certain over time”.
The new figures are likely to elevate the concerns from state governments about the impact on the hospital system from older Australians dropping out of private health.
The health ministers of NSW, Queensland and Tasmania told The Australian in July the “deeply concerning” decision to scrap the higher rebate for over-65s would put further pressure on their strained public hospital systems, in an escalation of national cabinet tensions.
Opposition health spokeswoman Anne Ruston said “Mark Butler has only ever told Australians that 44,000 older people would drop their cover”.
“His own department told him it would be 78,000. Either he didn’t read his own briefs, or he’s been deliberately misleading older Australians,” she said.
“Labor keeps saying this costs older Australians less than a dollar a day. The department’s own documents show a 70-year-old on gold cover could lose more than $600 a year, which is an annual power bill for a pensioner.
“If pensioners can’t afford to keep their cover, they don’t stop needing care. They put off treatment, get sicker, and end up on public hospital waiting lists that are already far too long.” An Albanese government spokeswoman said the proposed rebate overhaul was “about making the private health insurance rebates fairer”.
“Under the proposed changes, all Australians will now receive the same private health support, based on their income, not age,” the spokeswoman said.
“Under the proposed changes, over-65s will still receive significant government-subsidised discounts of up to 24 per cent on the premiums private health insurers charge them, the same as the rest of the population.
“The current additional rebate is simply not the best way to spend precious taxpayers’ dollars on behalf of older Australians when we need to do so much heavy lifting in aged care.
“Every dollar will be reinvested to deliver more aged care beds, more packages and better care for older Australians.” The government’s policy change, projected to raise $3bn over four years, would remove the higher rebates for over-65s that were introduced by the Howard government.
Under the existing system, families on the basic tier earning less than $202,000 a year (or singles earning less than $101,000) will receive a 24 per cent rebate if they are aged under 65, 28 per cent if they are aged 65-69 and 32 per cent for those over 70.
In tier two, singles earning $118-000-$158,000 or families on $236,000-$316,000 receive an 8 per cent rebate, rising to 12 per cent for 65 to 69-year-olds and 16 per cent for those over 70. Those earning more receive no rebate.
The policy is facing headwinds in parliament, with both the Coalition and Greens issuing dissenting reports after a Labor-led committee endorsed it.
The Greens said they had “serious concerns about the bill in its present form”. “Of particular concern are the impacts of these changes on specific cohorts, particularly the financial impact on people over 65 who are on low incomes, including pensioners and part-pensioners,” their dissenting report states.
